question: Sheep and goat farmers in Thessaly have been dealing with the spread of the plague or peste des petits ruminants (PPR) since 11 July. On 27 July, the virus hit Korinthia and on 29 July it reared its head in West Attica. It is the first time this contagious disease has been detected in Greece and the EU as a whole.

According to information provided by the competent veterinary services, the cases occurred as a result of animals being ‘legally’ imported from Romania, i.e. from another EU Member State. This is yet another instance of the detrimental effect the EU’s CAP policy is having on ordinary farmers, a policy which all Greek governments have implemented and helped shape.

Under the CAP, aside from any checks carried out in the ‘country of origin’, agricultural products, animals and goods coming from other Member States, enjoy ‘free entry’ without any checks or restrictions on the cross-border movement of these products, animals and goods. In this way, business groups secure raw materials by importing massively.

Losses already total nearly EUR 3 million since each animal costs around EUR 300, and that is not counting the loss of income suffered by the livestock farmers. Given that the EU bears huge responsibility for the current situation, since the spread of the disease and the destruction of livestock is a consequence of the CAP and of the ‘free’ movement of goods, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What measures will it take to fully compensate Greek livestock farmers for their losses, including loss of income?
What is its position concerning the urgent need for full staffing of State veterinary services and laboratories?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2024) In accordance with Regulation (EU) No 2021/6901 and Commission Implementing Decision C(2023) 89262, in particular Annex 3 thereof3, certain measures implemented by Greece against the Peste des petits ruminants (culling of animals, compensation to owners for the value of the animals culled, disinfections of holdings, etc.)
may be eligible for EU co-funding, up to a maximum rate of 30%.

Moreover, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/21154, depending on the identified needs and intervention strategy, through their Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans, Member States may provide support for investments in preventive actions and for restoration of agricultural potential following natural disasters, adverse climatic or catastrophic events5.

This would also allow to support investments to restore agricultural production potentially damaged by animal diseases or by measures taken to eradicate or contain the disease. The design and implementation of those measures depends on Member States.

Staffing of veterinary services and related laboratories in Member States, including Greece, is under the responsibility of each Member State, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2016/4296, in particular Article 13 thereof.
